claims.claim: Bishop of Alexandria after Theonas, from about 300; less than three years before the persecution
claims.witness: Eusebius, Church History VII.32, IX.6; Jerome, Chronicle

claims.claim: Wrote canons in 306 on receiving the lapsed, and would not condemn those who fled
claims.witness: Peter, Canonical Epistle (anf06), Canons I and XIII

claims.claim: Broke with Meletius of Lycopolis; wrote to Alexandria to hold no communion with him
claims.witness: Peter, Letter to the Church at Alexandria (anf06); letter of the four bishops (anf06)

claims.claim: Meletius was removed by a council under Peter for crimes including sacrifice to idols
claims.witness: Athanasius, Apology against the Arians 59; Socrates I.6; Theodoret I.8

claims.claim: The split began over how to receive the lapsed, with Peter and Meletius in prison together
claims.witness: Epiphanius, Panarion 68 (a pro-Meletian account, used by Bell)

claims.claim: Beheaded in the ninth year of the persecution, about 25 November 311
claims.witness: Eusebius IX.6; Bell 1924

claims.claim: Peter ordained Arius a deacon and later cast him out
claims.witness: Sozomen I.15 (one witness; Hartranft notes no one else links Arius with the Meletians early); Robertson doubts it

contested_claims.sides: Athanasius, Socrates and Theodoret (Meletius removed for crimes and sacrifice) against Epiphanius (Peter and Meletius jailed together, split over the lapsed, Peter for mercy). Bell reads them as stages of one quarrel; Hefele says the first letters show neither man was then in prison and that Epiphanius erred on the main points.

absent_details.note: No early source gives them. Later Coptic and Ethiopic lives supply a family and disagree with each other; Inferential-Thin at best, not used as fact.

claims.claim: Alexandrian by birth; first among his contemporaries in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic and physics
claims.witness: Eusebius, Church History VII.32; Jerome, Lives 73

claims.claim: Led people out of the besieged Pyrucheium quarter of Alexandria
claims.witness: Eusebius VII.32 ("They say")

claims.claim: Ordained bishop by Theotecnus at Caesarea, then made bishop of Laodicea on the way to the Antioch synod
claims.witness: Eusebius VII.32

claims.claim: Wrote Paschal Canons using a nineteen-year cycle, and ten books of arithmetic
claims.witness: Eusebius VII.32 (quoting the extract); anf06

claims.claim: The first Christian to use the nineteen-year cycle for Easter
claims.witness: Arthur McGiffert, note to Eusebius ("so far as we know")

claims.claim: The longer Latin book on Easter under his name is genuine
claims.witness: McGiffert, following Zahn, for; Ideler against

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Latin Paschal Canon (first printed 1634) is Anatolius's own work
contested_claims.sides: McGiffert, following Zahn, sees "the best of reasons" for an early translation of his genuine work; Ideler held it a seventh-century work. Only the extract Eusebius quotes, and the arithmetic fragments, are firm.

absent_details.note: No held source gives them. Richardson (born about 230, died about 283) and Salmond (230, 270, 280, called conjectural) only estimate; Eusebius says his death came before the persecution.

claims.claim: Bishop of Ephesus while Victor was bishop of Rome; led the bishops of Asia in the Easter dispute
claims.witness: Eusebius, Church History V.22-25; Jerome, Lives 45

claims.claim: Wrote to Victor defending the fourteenth-day Easter, citing the lights of Asia and his seven bishop relatives
claims.witness: Polycrates, letter in Eusebius V.24 and III.31

claims.claim: Victor cut off the churches of Asia from communion
claims.witness: Eusebius V.24 (McGiffert reads it as done; Socrates V.22 says so); Hefele, following Valesius, reads it as a threat only

claims.claim: The Philip buried at Hierapolis was the apostle
claims.witness: Polycrates in Eusebius; McGiffert holds it a confusion with Philip the evangelist; Lightfoot defends Polycrates

contested_claims.claim: Whether Victor actually excommunicated the churches of Asia
contested_claims.sides: McGiffert holds he did, and Socrates of Constantinople says so directly; Hefele, following Valesius, holds that Victor only threatened it and was held back by Irenaeus.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Philip at Hierapolis was the apostle or the evangelist
contested_claims.sides: Polycrates (and Eusebius) say the apostle; McGiffert holds it a confusion with Philip the evangelist of Acts; Lightfoot defends Polycrates.

absent_details.detail: Polycrates's birth, death and personal end
absent_details.note: McGiffert says the years of his accession and death are not known. The only dated claims (anf08 "about 200" and the editor's "130-196") are unsourced and disagree.

claims.claim: Roman governor of Bithynia from 110 or 111 who tried Christians and wrote to Trajan for guidance
claims.witness: Pliny, Letters 10.96, in McGiffert's note to Eusebius III.33

claims.claim: Reported Christians meeting before dawn to sing to Christ as God, and questioned two deaconesses under torture
claims.witness: Pliny, Letters 10.96, in McGiffert's note

claims.claim: Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, but punished if accused and convicted
claims.witness: Trajan, Letters 10.97, in McGiffert's note; Tertullian, Apology 2; Eusebius III.33

claims.claim: Nephew of Pliny the Elder and a friend of Trajan
claims.witness: McGiffert, note to Eusebius III.33

absent_details.detail: Pliny's birth and death years and his family
absent_details.note: No held primary source gives them. The only dated figures are in the secondary Malech (lived 61-115), unsourced. No held source attests his friendship with Tacitus.
